figures.title: The Flavorings Family Tree
figures.subtitle: Flavor is taste plus smell: five tastes, many aromas, and the label lines.

segments.name: Flavor
segments.text: This lesson is about flavor and flavorings. What we call flavor is mostly two senses working together: taste on the tongue and smell in the nose.

segments.name: Five Tastes
segments.text: Taste has five basic tastes, each with its own receptor: sweet, bitter, sour, salty and umami. Under each are the foods that trigger it.

segments.name: Smell and Labels
segments.text: Smell covers thousands of aromas, like vanilla, mint, citrus and cinnamon. And on the right are the flavor lines you see on a label: natural and artificial flavor. Each box links to its figure.

segments.name: Pinch Your Nose
segments.text: Try it: pinch your nose and a jelly bean tastes only sweet. Let go, and the cherry or lemon comes back. That's smell doing most of the work.

segments.name: Molecules Meet Receptors
segments.text: Every taste and smell starts when a molecule fits a receptor protein on a sensory cell. Most added flavorings are aroma molecules; a few, like MSG, act on taste.

figures.title: How Flavor Works
figures.subtitle: The five basic tastes, their receptors, and why smell does most of the work.

segments.name: Sweet and Umami
segments.text: Here are the five tastes. Sweet signals energy and umami signals protein, and they share a receptor part: T1R3 pairs with T1R2 for sweet and with T1R1 for umami.

segments.name: Salty, Sour, Bitter
segments.text: Salty signals sodium, a mineral we need. Sour signals acid, from unripe or spoiled food. And bitter warns of possible poisons, using about 25 different receptors.

segments.name: Smell
segments.text: Smell does most of the work. As you chew, aroma molecules rise from the back of your mouth into your nose, where about 400 kinds of receptor combine to tell a huge number of smells apart.

segments.name: Tongue Map Myth
segments.text: The tongue map you may have learned is a myth: every part with taste buds senses all five tastes. And taste cells are replaced every week or two.

segments.name: Hot and Cool
segments.text: Chili heat, mint cool and the fizz of soda aren't tastes or smells at all. They're touch and pain nerves reacting to chemicals, as we saw in Bioactives.

figures.title: Sweet and Bitter
figures.subtitle: One receptor for sweet, about 25 for bitter.

segments.name: Sucrose
segments.text: Table sugar is glucose and fructose joined through an oxygen. Its OH groups grip the sweet receptor's clamp-like pocket.

segments.name: One Sweet Receptor
segments.text: There's one sweet receptor, built from two proteins, and sugars, sweeteners and even a few plant proteins all fit it in different spots. Sweeteners like sucralose fit it hundreds of times more tightly, so a tiny amount tastes as sweet.

segments.name: Sweet Adapts
segments.text: Liking for sweetness falls when people eat less sugar for a few weeks. The WHO advises keeping free sugars below ten percent of calories.

segments.name: Many Bitter Receptors
segments.text: Bitter compounds like caffeine share no single shape, so we need about 25 kinds of bitter receptor to catch them. It's our most sensitive taste, because many plant poisons are bitter.

segments.name: Bitter Tasters
segments.text: People differ. About a quarter are strong tasters of certain bitter compounds, through a variant of one receptor, and often find broccoli, kale and grapefruit harsher. Salt, fat, sweetness and cooking all soften bitterness.

figures.title: Sour and Salty
figures.subtitle: Tastes made by ions: hydrogen and sodium.

segments.name: Hydrogen Ions
segments.text: Sour is the taste of acid. Acids release hydrogen ions, which in water ride on a water molecule as hydronium. Sour cells sense them through a channel called OTOP1 that lets them in.

segments.name: Citric Acid
segments.text: Citric acid, the sour of lemons, has three acid groups, each able to release a hydrogen ion. Acids are added to foods for tartness and to preserve them, though frequent acidic drinks can erode tooth enamel.

segments.name: Sodium
segments.text: Salt taste is mainly the taste of sodium ions, entering salt cells through a channel called ENaC. Very high salt also switches on bitter and sour cells, which is why heavily salted food tastes harsh.

segments.name: Salt Substitutes
segments.text: Potassium chloride, in salt substitutes, tastes salty but also bitter and metallic, because potassium doesn't fit the sodium channel as well.

segments.name: Less Salt
segments.text: The Daily Value for sodium is 2,300 milligrams, about a teaspoon of salt, and most comes from processed and restaurant food. Taste adapts: after a few weeks of eating less, lightly salted food tastes right.

figures.title: Umami and Glutamate
figures.subtitle: The savory taste, and the facts about MSG.

segments.name: Glutamate
segments.text: Glutamate is one of the amino acids in every protein. Free, unattached glutamate is what tastes savory, and the umami receptor grips its second acid group. MSG is just glutamate paired with sodium.

segments.name: Inosinate
segments.text: Inosinate, from meat and fish, binds the same receptor at a different spot and multiplies glutamate's effect. That's why dashi, or tomato with parmesan, tastes so rich.

segments.name: Discovery
segments.text: The Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda named umami in 1908 after finding glutamate in kombu seaweed broth, and went on to make MSG.

segments.name: MSG Safety
segments.text: The FDA lists MSG as generally recognized as safe, and controlled studies haven't consistently reproduced the symptoms people blame on it. Your body handles it like the glutamate in tomatoes. And it has about a third as much sodium as salt.

segments.name: Found In
segments.text: Glutamate is naturally high in parmesan, tomatoes, mushrooms, soy sauce, miso, fish sauce, kombu, yeast extract and broth.

segments.name: Vanillin
segments.text: Vanillin has an aldehyde on a ring, plus the methoxy and OH pair of guaiacol, the smoke molecule from Processing. It's the main flavor of cured vanilla beans, though less than one percent of vanillin actually comes from vanilla.

segments.name: Cinnamaldehyde
segments.text: Cinnamaldehyde is a ring, a double bond and an aldehyde. It's most of cinnamon's essential oil, and it switches on TRPA1, the receptor behind cinnamon's warm sting.

segments.name: Cassia Caution
segments.text: Cassia, the common cinnamon in North America, also contains coumarin, which can harm the liver in large amounts. Ceylon cinnamon has very little.

segments.name: Menthol
segments.text: Menthol is a carbon ring with one OH. It switches on TRPM8, the receptor that senses cold, so mint feels cool at room temperature.

segments.name: Limonene
segments.text: Limonene, from citrus peel, is a terpene built from two isoprene units. Its two mirror-image forms smell different: one of oranges, one more of pine.

figures.title: Natural vs Artificial Flavors
figures.subtitle: Identical molecules from different sources, and what the words mean.

segments.name: From Rice Bran
segments.text: Microbes can trim ferulic acid, from rice bran, down to vanillin. Because it starts from a plant and uses fermentation, the result can be called natural.

segments.name: From Petroleum
segments.text: Most vanillin is built from guaiacol made from petroleum. The vanillin is identical, molecule for molecule, but it must be called artificial.

segments.name: Ethyl Vanillin
segments.text: Ethyl vanillin has one extra carbon, doesn't occur in vanilla, and tastes two to four times stronger. It's always an artificial flavor.

segments.name: The Definitions
segments.text: In US rules, a natural flavor comes from a plant, animal or fermentation source; an artificial flavor is anything else. Natural and artificial versions of the same molecule act the same in the body. Natural describes the source, not the nutrition or the safety.

segments.name: Secret Recipes
segments.text: A natural flavor can be a mixture of dozens of compounds plus solvents and carriers, and the recipe doesn't have to be disclosed, although major allergens must be.

figures.title: Reading Flavor Lines on a Label
figures.subtitle: What each flavor-related ingredient line tells you.

segments.name: Flavor Lines
segments.text: Here's what the flavor lines on a label mean. Natural flavors come from plant, animal or fermentation sources; artificial flavors are synthesized, and when they supply the main flavor, the front must say artificially flavored.

segments.name: Vanilla and Spices
segments.text: Vanilla extract has a legal standard. Vanillin is artificial unless stated as natural. And spices can be listed as a group, except paprika, turmeric and saffron, which also add color.

segments.name: Umami Lines
segments.text: MSG must be named. Yeast extract and hydrolyzed protein are natural sources of free glutamate, so a food containing them can't claim no MSG. Smoke flavoring is filtered smoke.

segments.name: Front of Pack
segments.text: On the front, strawberry yogurt suggests real fruit, while strawberry flavored can mean the taste comes from flavorings, so check the ingredients. In the EU, natural vanilla flavouring must get at least 95 percent of its flavor from vanilla.

figures.title: Where flavorings are used in the body
figures.subtitle: Tap a number or a name to see what that place does with it.

segments.name: Where Flavorings Go
segments.text: Here's the statue with the places flavorings are used. Flavor is built in the mouth, the nose and the brain. After that, the molecules are digested and cleared like any other part of food. Tap a number to see what each place does.
segments.cue: The statue and its numbered places

segments.name: Taste, Smell and Feel
segments.text: Taste buds on the tongue sense sweet, bitter, sour, salty and umami. The nose has about 400 kinds of smell receptor, which pick up aromas from the front and from inside the mouth as you chew. The trigeminal nerve senses the cool of menthol and the bite of mustard.
segments.cue: Numbers 1 to 3: tongue, nose and mouth nerves

foodBody.name: Vanillin
foodBody.text: The main flavor of vanilla, natural or made in a factory. A smell receptor in your nose detects it; the liver then clears it like other food molecules.

foodBody.name: Menthol
foodBody.text: In mint. It triggers TRPM8, the cold receptor, so mint feels cool.

segments.name: The Brain
segments.text: The brain combines taste, smell, texture and heat into the single experience we call flavor. That's why food tastes flat when your nose is blocked.

foodBody.name: Aroma molecules
foodBody.text: The small molecules that give food its smell, like vanillin in vanilla. As you chew, they rise up the back of your nose to smell receptors that signal the brain.

segments.name: Digested and Cleared
segments.text: Flavor molecules are swallowed and absorbed like the rest of the food; the gut even has taste receptors of its own. The liver breaks most of them down, and the kidneys send the products out in urine.
segments.cue: Numbers 5 to 7: gut, liver and kidneys

foodBody.name: Flavorings
foodBody.text: Natural and artificial flavorings are used in tiny amounts. Your gut absorbs them, the liver changes most of them so they dissolve in water, and the kidneys pass them out in urine.

segments.name: Simplified
segments.text: This is simplified. Flavorings are used in tiny amounts, so the numbers mark where they act, not a dose.

figures.title: Putting It All Together
figures.subtitle: The whole lesson in one table, plus a few extras.

segments.name: One Table
segments.text: Here's the whole lesson in one table: each taste, aroma and label line, with its molecules, receptor, main sources, and what's good to know.

segments.name: Worth Knowing
segments.text: A few extras. Losing your sense of smell makes food seem tasteless even though taste works; herbs, spices and acidity can help instead of more salt and sugar. Researchers are studying possible extra tastes, like kokumi and fat. And the pleasure of one flavor fades as you eat it, which is why there's always room for dessert.
